landmarks.name: Blue Lagoon
landmarks.writeup: A geothermal spa known for its milky blue waters rich in minerals, located in a lava field.

wiki.extract: The Blue Lagoon is a geothermal spa in southwestern Iceland. The spa is located in a lava field 5 km (3.1 mi) from Grindavík and in front of Mount Þorbjörn on the Reykjanes Peninsula, in a location favourable for geothermal power, and is supplied by water used in the nearby Svartsengi geothermal power station. The Blue Lagoon is approximately 20 km (12 mi) from Keflavík International Airport, and is one of the most visited tourist attractions in Iceland.

landmarks.name: Thingvellir National Park
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates meet.

wiki.extract: Þingvellir was the site of the Alþing, the annual parliament of Iceland from the year 930 until the last session held at Þingvellir in 1798. Since 1881, the parliament has been located within Alþingishúsið in Iceland's capital, Reykjavík.

landmarks.name: Geysir Geothermal Area
landmarks.writeup: Famous for its erupting hot springs, including the active Strokkur geyser.

wiki.extract: Geysir, sometimes known as The Great Geysir, is a geyser in south-western Iceland, that geological studies suggest started forming about 1150 CE. The English word geyser derives from Geysir. The name Geysir itself is derived from the Icelandic verb geysa. Geysir lies in the Haukadalur valley on the slopes of Laugarfjall lava dome, which is also the home to Strokkur geyser about 50 metres (160 ft) to the south. The Strokkur geyser may be confused with it, and the geothermal field it is in is known usually as either Geysir or Haukadalur.

landmarks.name: Hallgrímskirkja
landmarks.writeup: A distinctive Lutheran church in Reykjavik, known for its unique architecture and panoramic city views.

wiki.extract: Hallgrímskirkja is a Protestant Lutheran parish church in Reykjavík, Iceland. At 74.5 metres (244 ft) tall, it is the largest church in Iceland and second tallest building in the country. Known for its distinctively curved spire and side wings, it has been described as having become an important symbol for Iceland's national identity since its completion in 1986. The church is named after the Icelandic poet and cleric Hallgrímur Pétursson (1614–1674), author of the Passion Hymns.

landmarks.name: Vatnajökull National Park
landmarks.writeup: Home to Europe's largest glacier and diverse volcanic landscapes.

wiki.extract: Vatnajökull National Park is one of three national parks in Iceland, and is the largest one. It encompasses all of Vatnajökull glacier and extensive surrounding areas. These include the national parks previously existing at Skaftafell in the southwest and Jökulsárgljúfur in the north.

cultural_events.name: Iceland Airwaves
cultural_events.writeup: An annual music festival showcasing Icelandic and international artists.

wiki.extract: Iceland Airwaves is a music festival held annually in November in Reykjavík, Iceland, since 1999. Its main focus is showcasing new music, both Icelandic and international.

cultural_events.name: Þorrablót
cultural_events.writeup: A midwinter festival celebrating traditional Icelandic food and heritage.

wiki.extract: Þorrablót is an Icelandic midwinter festival, named for the month of Þorri of the historical Icelandic calendar, and blót, literally meaning sacrifice.

cultural_events.name: Reykjavik International Film Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An event promoting independent films from around the world.

wiki.extract: Reykjavík International Film Festival is an international film festival held annually in Reykjavík, Iceland. The festival lasts 11 days each year and emphasizes young talents. One way of doing so is having a competitive category exclusively limited to a director's first or second feature-length film. At each festival, a number of awards are given out. The main award is the Discovery of the Year award, also called Golden Puffin, given by an international jury. The international federation of film critics FIPRESCI send a jury to RIFF from 2006. Also, the audience can vote for their favorite film from the whole programme. Lifetime achievement awards and creative excellence awards are given to well-known film directors who have achieved excellence in their work.

cultural_events.name: National Day
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on June 17th, marking Iceland's independence from Denmark in 1944.

wiki.extract: A national day is a day on which celebrations mark the statehood or nationhood of a state or its people. It may be the date of independence, of becoming a republic, of becoming a federation, or a significant date for a patron saint, a ruler or a date in that country's particular history.

cultural_events.name: Winter Lights Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A festival celebrating the return of light with art, culture, and outdoor activities.

wiki.extract: The Winter Festival of Lights in Niagara Falls, Ontario, is Canada's largest lights festival. It runs from mid-November to mid-January and attracts over one million visitors annually. The event has free admission while accepting voluntary donations. As of 2023, it features a decorated eight-kilometre route along the Niagara Parkway that extends into the tourist districts and the Dufferin Islands. The lights are installed and run by Ontario Power Generation.

food_writeup: Icelandic cuisine features fresh seafood, lamb, and dairy products, with traditional dishes like skyr, hákarl (fermented shark), and rye bread. The cuisine reflects the island's Nordic heritage and reliance on local ingredients.
brief_history: Iceland was settled by Norsemen in the 9th century. It established a commonwealth in 930 AD, later coming under Norwegian and then Danish rule. Iceland gained full independence in 1944 and has developed a strong economy based on fishing, renewable energy, and tourism.

commentary.inflation_management: The Central Bank of Iceland targets 2.5%, but the small, open economy with its own floating currency produces chronic overshoots. Inflation was 12.7% in 2008 (the series high) and 12% in 2009 as the krona collapsed, fell to 1.6% in 2015 (the low), ran hot again at 8.3% in 2022 on the energy shock, then 5.9% in 2024 and a projected 4.1% for 2025 — persistently above target. The bank has hiked aggressively in each cycle, and krona depreciation repeatedly feeds imported inflation. The 2010s experiment with the currency showed the float cushions output but punishes price stability.
commentary.debt_management: Iceland's debt went from 69.8% of GDP in 2006 to 136.6% in 2011, the series peak, as the state absorbed the cost of the banking collapse — then one of history's fastest consolidations brought it to a projected 56.1% in 2025, the series low (76.1% in 2020, 66.4% in 2022). GDP grew from $17.7bn in 2006 to a projected $38.6bn in 2025. The clean-up worked: banking-sector liabilities were ring-fenced, capital controls were lifted in 2017, and growth plus surpluses did the rest. Iceland is the counter-example to the idea that banking crises must leave permanent debt.

key_events.event: Banking collapse (October 2008): the three big banks failed; IMF program and capital controls followed.
Inflation peaked at 12.7% on krona collapse; the Icesave dispute with the UK and Netherlands.
Debt peaked at 136.6% of GDP as crisis costs were absorbed.
Capital controls lifted (2017) after the crisis-era balance-of-payments was stabilized.
COVID-19: tourism collapse pushed debt to 76.1% of GDP; recovery was swift.
Inflation back above target at 4.1% projected for 2025; debt at the series low of 56.1%.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Iceland's macro fundamentals are strong: low debt, flexible exchange rate, abundant renewable energy, and a recovered tourism sector. The persistent issue is above-target inflation, which keeps real rates high and the krona volatile — a structural feature of the small currency, not a policy failure. Growth prospects are solid on energy-intensive industry and fisheries; the binding risks are external shocks to tourism and the chronic inflation overshoot eroding competitiveness. Debt at 56% of GDP gives ample fiscal room.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
